I welcome Ms. Gagnon, who is in Kabul, and I give her the floor.  
Ms. Gagnon : Last month, the de facto authorities marked the fifth year of their 
return to power. They projected confidence, highlighting nationwide control, improved 
security, infrastructure development and economic stabilization efforts as evidence of 
their success . They also launched an initiative to improve institutional openness and 
accountability. These developments are encouraging. They are occurring, however, in a 
context of no progress on issues that are of profound concern to the Afghan people and 
the intern ational community: the severe restrictions on women and girls, exclusionary 
governance, a human rights crisis and the continued presence of terrorist groups that 
threaten Afghanistan, the region and international peace and security.  
In line with my most recent briefing to this Council (see S/PV.10165), we assess 
that the de facto authorities face no significant armed or political threat. However, key 
risks to the country’s stability are accumulating and mainly stem from the de facto 
authorities’ own policies. Recent events in Badakhshan Province illustrate these risks. 
While the armed clashes, as detailed in the Secretary -General’s report (S/2026/724), did 
not threaten de facto authority control, they show what can happen when local 
communities are excluded from decision -making, resource -sharing and economic 
opportunity. During my recent visit to Badakhshan, people told me they seek 
opportunities, basic services, education and a future for their children, not exclusion.  
Over the past three months, events in Herat Province remained similarly 
concerning. The United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) 
documented arrests of women and girls related to strict enforcement of the de facto 
authorities’ dress code. Su bsequent protests were met with an excessive use of force. 
The de facto authorities continue to carry out arrests of women, including over the past 
week, for alleged violation of the dress code. Across the country, UNAMA also 
documented mounting pressure o n minority communities, media outlet closures and 
arrests and intimidation of journalists. These incidents are part of the broader trend of 
coercive social regulation that is alienating many communities. UNAMA is engaging

This month, UNAMA released a report on the experiences of victims of 
Afghanistan’s decades -long conflict. Ninety -five per cent of the people we interviewed 
in Afghanistan reported continued psychological and emotional harm, including 
depression, anxiety, t rauma and flashbacks. Many are still living with disability, chronic 
pain and loss of livelihoods. The findings remind us that peace is not only the absence 
of armed conflict. Sustainable peace requires dignity, inclusion, opportunity and hope. 
Many Afghan s tell us that the past five years of relative stability have provided a 
welcome breathing space. Yet they also tell us they are suffering under the rigid social 
policies of the de facto authorities and as a result of Afghanistan’s fragile economic and 
humanitarian situation.  
While Afghanistan has maintained a degree of macroeconomic stability, this does 
not equate to recovery. Economic growth has not kept pace with a rising population or 
made up for declining aid. Per capita income has dropped by 5.6 per cent, and exports 
are down. Afghanistan remains heavily dependent on imports, with border disruptions 
and wider regional instability contributing to weakened household purchasing power. 
Food insecurity and malnutrition present a serious concern. UNICEF reports that some 
3.7 mil lion children are suffering from deficient malnutrition, including some 1 million 
children experiencing severe acute malnutrition. The 2026 humanitarian needs and 
response plan is only 30 per cent funded. Humanitarian organizations are being forced 
to make  hard choices on where they operate, whom they can reach and which services 
they can maintain. Health facilities, nutrition centres, women’s protection services and 
other essential programmes have closed or scaled back due to funding cuts.  
At the same time, Afghanistan continues to experience an extreme demographic 
and socioeconomic shock. This year alone, nearly 1.2 million Afghans have returned 
from Pakistan and Iran, with total returns reaching 6.5 million since 2023. Without 
sustained su pport for returnees and host communities, competition over scarce resources 
risks fuelling grievances, increasing displacement and promoting instability. The de 
facto authorities’ ban on opium poppy cultivation has been a positive measure, with 
huge decrea ses in cultivation but risks bouncing back because of the economic pressures. 
Greater support for alternative livelihoods is crucial, as is sustained and principled 
humanitarian and development assistance for the Afghan people.  
No discussion of Afghanistan can ignore the continued exclusion of women and 
girls. The words of an Afghan woman we met in Kandahar represents their experience:  
“If we follow one rule, another one comes next. Women wearing hijab are 
instructed to wear a mask; those wearing masks are told to wear a burka; those 
wearing a burka are questioned about the absence of a mahram; and those 
accompanied by a mahram are quest ioned about the relationship with him.”  
By denying women access to education, professions and public life, the de facto 
authorities are not safeguarding Afghanistan’s future; they are constraining the talent 
and productivity needed for post -conflict recovery. This is at odds with their stated 
vision of a prosperous, self -reliant and sovereign Afghanistan that can attract 
international investment. This month marks one year since restrictions preventing 
Afghan women from accessing United Nations premises, including national female 
United Nations pe rsonnel, were enforced. This is a violation of United Nations 
principles and a serious operational constraint. Humanitarian actors report difficulty 
reaching women and girls. Male -only delivery models cannot replace the participation 
of Afghan women staff,  and organizations cannot consult women, assess risks or verify 
that assistance reaches those who need it most.

Funding cuts are compounding the problem. Nearly three quarters of Afghan 
women-led organizations have seen reduced funding over the past year, while more than 
80 per cent report increasing needs among women and girls. At a moment when Afghan 
women face un precedented restrictions, international support mechanisms for them are 
decreasing. Across Afghanistan, Afghan women tell us that engagement, assistance and 
support from the international community represent what they call points of hope. We 
urge internati onal partners to prioritize support for Afghan women and girls. Above all, 
we again call on the de facto authorities to end all restrictions on women and girls.  
Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan remain another matter of serious 
concern. The effects of sporadic hostilities and the almost year -long border closure are 
taking an increasing toll on civilians, communities and businesses. UNAMA continues 
to enco urage de -escalation and dialogue to resolve differences, including on the 
presence of terrorist groups in Afghanistan, as reported by the Sanctions Monitoring 
Team. We welcome ongoing regional mediation efforts.  
As the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the United Nations 
Development Programme Administrator cautioned during a joint visit to Afghanistan in 
July, developments in Afghanistan do not necessarily stay in Afghanistan. Instability, 
increase d out -migration and displacement, radicalization and growing insecurity have 
regional and international consequences. Sustained international engagement, including 
through the Doha process, remains essential. Currently, the Doha process is the 
multilateral  framework through which such engagement is occurring, aimed at 
Afghanistan’s reintegration into the international community on the basis of compliance 
with international obligations and commitments. This structured engagement among the 
de facto authoritie s, the international community and a wide range of Afghan 
stakeholders has identified key issues and positions, expanded dialogue and, in some 
areas, built confidence.  
The main obstacle to progress is the de facto authorities’ preference for bilateral 
approaches over multilateral engagement, which they view as undermining their claims 
of sovereignty. They continue, however, to participate in working groups on counter -
narcotics in the private sector and engage on some key political issues. What is now 
needed is a clear indication from the de facto authorities of their willingness to address 
the wider concerns of the international community. To this end, the de facto author ities 
can take steps towards inclusive governance and the lifting of restrictions on women 
and girls and show they are meeting their counter -terrorism commitments. Member 
States can reinforce that Afghanistan’s reintegration into the international system i s 
possible through concrete, balanced, cooperative steps that begin to address the key 
issues preventing reintegration. We remain confident in the value of principled and 
pragmatic engagement. It sustains dialogue on the key issues and concerns, maintains 
influence, reduces risks, creates opportunities for progress and critically supports the 
needs and aspirations of the Afghan people.

Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, we also witnessed the erosion of universal values, 
internatio nal commitments and, most profoundly, the norms and standards for the 
protection of the human rights and dignity of women.

Addressing women’s rights cannot be separated from inclusive Government and inclusi ve

women and men, across ethnic and religious lines, can chart a shared vision for our country. 
Today, Afghan political actors, civil society and women are building a genuin e unity of

For five years, Afghan women have not been passive victims. We have organized,

Governments, parliaments, the United Nations and this chamber. At the moment we are

increasing risks and declining resources. The past five years have been highly

According to the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, 
Afghanistan’s humanitarian response plan for 2026 requires approximately $1.7 billion, 
yet only a small fraction of that requirement has been funded. This raises a fundamental 
question a bout the international community’s response. Can we honestly say that our 
response has gone beyond statements and expressions of concern?  
Solidarity must produce action. Afghan women cannot afford another year of 
waiting for the world to decide what to do with Afghanistan, how to deal with the 
Taliban and whether or not to support Afghan women. We need clarity, political will and 
a pathway f rom commitment to action, and we need it now.  
I therefore put forward three concrete proposals for the Council.  
First, a resolution should be adopted, recognizing the institutionalized 
discrimination against women and girls in Afghanistan and declaring the Council’s 
commitment to support us in our pursuit of justice and accountability. The resolution 
should also ask  Australia, Canada, Germany and the Netherlands to speed up the case 
of Afghanistan before the International Court of Justice, ask the International Criminal 
Court to issue more arrest warrants against the leadership of the Taliban and ask Member 
States to  recognize the situation in Afghanistan as gender apartheid and codify it as a 
crime against humanity.

Thirdly, we call on the international community to scale up humanitarian support 
to Afghanistan and fully fund the $1.7 billion response plan as an urgent priority. The 
support should target those most left behind.  
The world knows what is happening in Afghanistan. The question is whether the 
international community is prepared to act on what it knows or not.
